concept.name: Sliding Window Maximum Patterns

relationships.description: Connects Sliding Window Maximum Patterns to core algorithm patterns in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Sliding Window Maximum computes the maximum element in every contiguous subarray of size `k` across a length-`n` sequence in optimal $O(n)$ time and $O(k)$ space. By maintaining a monotonically decreasing double-ended queue (`deque`) of array indices, each element is pushed and popped at most once, beating naive $O(nk)$ scans and $O(n \log k)$ max-heaps.
spark.keyTakeaway: Store indices—not values—in a monotonically decreasing deque, evicting out-of-window indices from the front and smaller values from the back to hit strict $O(n)$ time.

concept.whyItMatters: Real-time stream processors (Apache Flink, Kafka Streams), network anomaly detectors, and financial tick engines continuously compute rolling peak CPU, peak latency, or max bid price over trailing `k`-event or `W`-second windows. At 100,000 events/sec with `k = 10,000`, an $O(n \cdot k)$ rescan executes $10^9$ comparisons per second and collapses, whereas a monotonic deque processes each event in amortized $O(1)$ time with predictable tail latency.
whenToUse: Fixed-size (`k`) or time-bounded rolling max/min queries over streaming or array data where $O(n)$ throughput is required.
Dynamic programming optimizations (e.g., Jump Game VI / constrained subsequence sum) where `dp[i]` depends on `max(dp[i-k ... i-1])`.
Telemetry and alerting pipelines tracking trailing peak utilization without retaining full sorted window state.
whenNotToUse: When you need arbitrary order statistics like rolling median, p95, or top-K elements (use two heaps, an order-statistic tree, or DDSketch/t-digest).
Static offline arrays with arbitrary variable-length `[L, R]` range max queries (use a Sparse Table for $O(1)$ query after $O(n \log n)$ build, or a Segment Tree if point updates occur).
Out-of-order event streams with late arrivals where elements cannot be appended monotonically at the window tail (requires a Segment Tree or Windowed Pane aggregation).
keyPoints: Store **indices** in the deque rather than raw values so you can check window expiration in $O(1)$ via `deque[0] <= i - k`.

Maintain the monotonic decreasing invariant: before pushing index `i`, pop all back indices `j` where `nums[j] <= nums[i]` because `j` is both smaller and older, so it can never be the max of any future window.
Amortized $O(1)$ per step: every index enters the back of the deque once and leaves either the front (expired) or back (dominated) at most once, yielding `<= 2n` deque operations total.
The front of the deque (`nums[deque[0]]`) is always the exact maximum of the current window once `i >= k - 1`.
A two-pass prefix/suffix block-max algorithm also achieves $O(n)$ time with $O(n)$ space and zero deque pointer chasing, ideal for SIMD/GPU batch arrays.

examples.title: Rolling Peak Latency Guard in a Stream Processor
examples.scenario: An observability service evaluates `max(latency_ms)` over a sliding window of the last 5,000 API requests per tenant to trigger circuit-breaker alerts.
examples.outcome: Replacing a `PriorityQueue` (which accumulated stale deleted nodes and triggered GC pauses) with a bounded ring-buffer monotonic deque cut p99 processing time per event from 4.2 µs to 0.18 µs.

examples.title: Bounded-Jump Dynamic Programming Optimization
examples.scenario: A DP recurrence `dp[i] = score[i] + max(dp[i-k ... i-1])` with `n = 100,000` and `k = 50,000` timed out at $O(n \cdot k) = 5 \times 10^9$ operations.
examples.outcome: Applying a monotonic decreasing deque over `dp` indices reduced the transition loop from $O(k)$ to amortized $O(1)$, solving all 100k states in 12 ms.

tradeOffs.pro: Monotonic deque achieves strict $O(n)$ time and bounded $O(k)$ memory.
tradeOffs.con: Max-heap is easier to adapt if arbitrary elements inside the window can be invalidated out of order, at the cost of $O(n \log n)$ worst-case heap growth.

tradeOffs.factor: Monotonic Deque vs Two-Pass Block Max (Prefix/Suffix)
tradeOffs.pro: Monotonic deque works online/streaming in $O(k)$ space without knowing `n` upfront.
tradeOffs.con: Block max requires $O(n)$ offline array storage, though it vectorizes cleanly.

tradeOffs.factor: Popping `<=` vs `<` at the back of the deque
tradeOffs.pro: Popping `nums[back] <= nums[i]` keeps the deque minimal and discards older duplicates.
tradeOffs.con: If a problem requires counting occurrences of the maximum or tie-breaking by earliest index, you must use strict `<` instead.

failureModes.name: Storing Values Instead of Indices
failureModes.description: Storing raw values in the deque makes it impossible to distinguish whether a duplicate value at `deque[0]` belongs to the expired element `nums[i - k]` or a newer occurrence inside the window.
failureModes.mitigation: Always store integer indices (or `(timestamp, value)` pairs for time-based windows) in the deque.

failureModes.name: Off-by-One Window Eviction
failureModes.description: Checking `deque[0] < i - k` instead of `<=` retains a `k+1`-element window, returning stale maxima from one step too far back.
failureModes.mitigation: For a 0-indexed window `[i - k + 1, i]`, evict while `deque[0] <= i - k` (equivalently `deque[0] < i - k + 1`).

failureModes.name: Unbounded Heap Memory Leak
failureModes.description: Using a max-heap with lazy deletion on a monotonically increasing stream (`[1, 2, 3, ...]`) or descending stream (`[n, n-1, ...]`) causes expired elements to stay buried in the heap, growing memory from $O(k)$ to $O(n)$.
failureModes.mitigation: Use a monotonic deque (hard-capped at `k` elements) instead of a lazy-deletion heap.

failureModes.name: Edge-Case `k == 0` or `k > n` Panic
failureModes.description: Indexing `deque[0]` on empty input (`n == 0`) or `k == 0` throws an index-out-of-bounds error.
failureModes.mitigation: Guard upfront: return `[]` if `n == 0` or `k == 0`, and clamp `k = min(k, n)` if partial windows are desired.

commonMistakes: Using `list.pop(0)` in Python instead of `collections.deque.popleft()`, silently degrading the algorithm from $O(n)$ to $O(n \cdot k)$.
Forgetting to check `i >= k - 1` before appending `nums[deque[0]]` to the result array, emitting partial-window maxima for the first `k - 1` elements.
Evicting from the front *after* reading the maximum instead of *before* (or right after pushing `i`), returning an expired element.
Assuming a monotonic deque can compute the sliding window *sum* or *average* (use a simple running sum for $O(1)$ space instead).
Applying the algorithm blindly to out-of-order time-series events without first watermarking/sorting by event timestamp.

sections.content:
## Pruning dominated candidates with a monotonic deque

When a window slides right by one element `nums[i]`, any older element `nums[j]` (`j < i`) inside the window that satisfies `nums[j] <= nums[i]` is **permanently dominated**: `nums[i]` is both larger (or equal) and will expire *later* than `nums[j]`. Therefore, `nums[j]` can never be the maximum of the current window or any future window. By popping all dominated elements from the back of a double-ended queue (`deque`) before appending `i`, the deque remains strictly decreasing in value and strictly increasing in index.

edges.label: Advance index i
edges.title: Check expiration
edges.description: Tests whether the oldest index at the front of the deque has fallen outside [i-k+1, i].

edges.label: popleft() if expired
edges.title: Evict stale front
edges.description: Removes at most one expired index from the front in O(1) time.

edges.label: Pop back <= nums[i]
edges.title: Prune dominated tail
edges.description: Discards all back indices whose values are <= nums[i] since they can never win.

edges.label: append(i)
edges.title: Preserve invariant
edges.description: Appends current index i to the back, keeping values strictly decreasing left-to-right.

edges.label: Read nums[dq[0]]
edges.title: Emit window max
edges.description: Once i >= k - 1, the front index always points to the maximum in the active window.

data.caption: Each index enters the deque once and is removed at most once (either expired at the front or dominated at the back), guaranteeing O(n) total work.

sections.content:
## Why the nested `while` loop is still $O(n)$

Although the algorithm places a `while` loop inside a `for` loop (`while dq and nums[dq[-1]] <= nums[i]: dq.pop()`), the total number of `pop()` operations across the *entire* run cannot exceed `n`, because each of the `n` indices is pushed onto `dq` exactly once. Combined with at most `n` `popleft()` operations, total deque work is bounded by `2n`—giving strict $O(n)$ worst-case time. Auxiliary space is bounded by $O(k)$ because `popleft()` ensures `dq` never spans more than `k` indices.

## Trade-offs across sliding-window maximum techniques

| Approach | Time Complexity | Space Complexity | Streaming? | Best Use Case |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Monotonic Deque** | $O(n)$ | $O(k)$ | Yes | Standard online & interview optimal solution |
| **Max-Heap (Lazy Delete)** | $O(n \log n)$ worst | $O(n)$ worst | Yes | Multi-order queries or out-of-order deletions |
| **Two-Pass Block DP** | $O(n)$ | $O(n)$ | No (needs `n`) | Vectorized / SIMD offline array processing |
| **Segment Tree / Sparse Table** | $O(n \log n)$ | $O(n)$ / $O(n \log n)$ | No | Arbitrary variable-length `[L, R]` queries |
| **Brute Force Scan** | $O(n \cdot k)$ | $O(1)$ | Yes | Tiny windows (`k <= 8`) with zero allocation |

## Bugs that break correctness or complexity

1. **ArrayDeque / List Front-Pop Penalty:** Using `ArrayList.remove(0)` in Java or `list.pop(0)` in Python shifts $O(k)$ elements on every eviction, turning $O(n)$ into $O(n \cdot k)$.
2. **Time-Based Window Skew:** In real-world streaming (e.g., max CPU in the last 60 seconds), the window size is measured in timestamps (`ts[i] - ts[dq[0]] >= 60_000`) rather than fixed index count `k`. Confusing count-based and time-based eviction breaks bursty streams.
3. **Integer Overflow in Comparator:** In Java/C++, subtracting `nums[dq.peekLast()] - nums[i]` overflows on `Integer.MIN_VALUE`; always use direct `<` / `<=` comparisons.

## Reference Python & Java idioms

In Python, use `collections.deque()` (doubly-linked block list, $O(1)$ at both ends): `if dq and dq[0] <= i - k: dq.popleft()` followed by `while dq and nums[dq[-1]] <= nums[i]: dq.pop()`. In Java, use `ArrayDeque<Integer>` (cache-friendly circular array, faster than `LinkedList` and zero per-node GC overhead): `peekFirst()`, `pollFirst()`, `peekLast()`, `pollLast()`, and `offerLast(i)`. For high-frequency telemetry in Java/Go, replace boxed `Integer` objects with a primitive `int[]` ring buffer of capacity `k + 1` to achieve zero heap allocations per event.

## Implementation & verification checklist

- [ ] **Store indices (or `(ts, val)`):** Never store raw values alone in the deque.
- [ ] **Evict before or right after window check:** Use `dq[0] <= i - k` for 0-indexed fixed windows of size `k`.
- [ ] **Use $O(1)$ double-ended queue:** `collections.deque` (Python) or `ArrayDeque` / primitive ring buffer (Java).
- [ ] **Verify `<=` vs `<`:** Use `<=` to keep the deque minimal; switch to `<` only if duplicates/earliest-index ties matter.
- [ ] **Handle boundary inputs:** Test `n == 0`, `k == 1`, `k == n`, strictly increasing, strictly decreasing, and all-equal arrays.
- [ ] **Emit only full windows:** Append to result only when `i >= k - 1`.

interviewProblems.title: Sliding Window Maximum Patterns
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Sliding Window Maximum Patterns. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Sliding Window Maximum computes the maximum element in every contiguous subarray of size `k` across a length-`n` sequence in optimal $O(n)$ time and $O(k)$ space. By maintaining a monotonically decreasing double-ended queue (`deque`) of array indices, each element is pushed and popped at most once, beating naive $O(nk)$ scans and $O(n \log k)$ max-heaps.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Monotonic Deque applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Window Max Output.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Window Max Output experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Always store integer indices (or `(timestamp, value)` pairs for time-based windows) in the deque.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Store indices—not values—in a monotonically decreasing deque, evicting out-of-window indices from the front and smaller values from the back to hit strict $O(n)$ time.
Avoid trap: Using `list.pop(0)` in Python instead of `collections.deque.popleft()`, silently degrading the algorithm from $O(n)$ to $O(n \cdot k)$.
Avoid trap: Forgetting to check `i >= k - 1` before appending `nums[deque[0]]` to the result array, emitting partial-window maxima for the first `k - 1` elements.
When to reach for it: Fixed-size (`k`) or time-bounded rolling max/min queries over streaming or array data where $O(n)$ throughput is required.
When to reach for it: Dynamic programming optimizations (e.g., Jump Game VI / constrained subsequence sum) where `dp[i]` depends on `max(dp[i-k ... i-1])`.

putItTogether.title: Putting Sliding Window Maximum Together
putItTogether.summary: Store indices—not values—in a monotonically decreasing deque, evicting out-of-window indices from the front and smaller values from the back to hit strict $O(n)$ time.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Sliding Window Maximum before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Replacing a `PriorityQueue` (which accumulated stale deleted nodes and triggered GC pauses) with a bounded ring-buffer monotonic deque cut p99 processing time per event from 4.2 µs to 0.18 µs.
